content: Morphea, also referred to as localized scleroderma, is a condition characterized by the thickening and hardening of the skin and underlying subcutaneous tissues due to excessive collagen deposition. This condition encompasses a spectrum of presentations, ranging from small, localized plaques affecting only the skin to more extensive disease that can result in significant functional impairment and cosmetic deformities. Unlike systemic sclerosis, morphea is generally confined to isolated patches of hardened skin and is not typically associated with internal organ involvement. Morphea is classified into five primary subtypes: plaque morphea, generalized morphea, linear scleroderma, bullous morphea, and deep morphea. However, this classification does not account for the mixed form of morphea, where multiple morphologies of skin lesions coexist in the same individual. Approximately 15% of patients with morphea may fall into this mixed category, which has only recently been recognized. Morphea is considered an uncommon condition, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 100,000 individuals. However, the true incidence and prevalence remain unclear due to a lack of comprehensive studies. It is also likely underreported, as smaller plaques may not prompt referral to specialists, and some physicians may be unfamiliar with the disorder. Similar to other connective tissue and autoimmune diseases, morphea predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:1. The exact cause of morphea remains unknown. Observational studies and case reports suggest a higher prevalence of autoimmune diseases in the family histories of patients with morphea. Autoantibody testing has revealed increased frequencies of anti-histone and anti-topoisomerase IIa antibodies in affected individuals. Additionally, morphea has been reported to coexist with other systemic autoimmune diseases, such as primary biliary cirrhosis, vitiligo, and systemic lupus erythematosus, supporting the hypothesis that morphea may have an autoimmune etiology. The diagnosis of morphea must be carefully distinguished from other conditions that may present with similar clinical features. These include annular lichenoid dermatitis of youth, ataxia-telangiectasia, atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini, carcinoid syndrome, cheiroarthropathy due to diabetes mellitus, eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, eosinophilic fasciitis, erythema migrans, fixed drug eruption, graft-versus-host disease, inflammatory granuloma annulare, interstitial and granulomatous dermatitis, interstitial mycosis fungoides, keloids and hypertrophic scars, lichen sclerosus et atrophicus, linear atrophoderma of Moulin, linear lupus erythematosus panniculitis, linear melorheostosis, lipodermatosclerosis, morpheaform dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, Muckle-Wells syndrome, nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy, Niemann-Pick disease, phenylketonuria, POEMS syndrome, porphyria cutanea tarda, primary systemic amyloidosis, progeria, radiation fibrosis, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, restrictive dermopathy, scleroderma, sclerodermoid conditions caused by chemical or toxin exposures (e.g., polyvinyl chloride, epoxy resins, pesticides, dry cleaning solvents, silica dust), sclerodermoid conditions caused by iatrogenic agents (e.g., bleomycin, gemcitabine, L-tryptophan, melphalan, pentazocine injections, silicone or paraffin implants, taxanes, uracil-tegafur, vitamin K injections), scleromyxedema, stiff skin syndrome, early Sweet syndrome, Werner syndrome, and Winchester syndrome. Over the years, various treatments have been explored for morphea, including topical, intralesional, and systemic corticosteroids. Antimalarial agents such as hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine have also been utilized. Other immunomodulatory therapies, including methotrexate, topical tacrolimus, and penicillamine, have been tried. Phototherapy with ultraviolet A (UVA) light, with or without psoralens, has been employed as well. UVA-1, a specific wavelength of UVA light, is thought to penetrate deeper into the skin and may soften morphea plaques through two mechanisms: (1) inducing systemic immunosuppression via UV light exposure and (2) activating enzymes that degrade the collagen matrix in the skin as part of the natural photoaging process. However, the lack of objective outcome measures has made it challenging to interpret the efficacy of these treatment modalities in clinical studies.
